title: Why long-term rates can rise while the Fed stands still
layers: The 10-year Treasury yield is set by investors buying and selling bonds every day, not by the Fed. It can rise even while the Fed holds its own rate steady.

A long-term yield is roughly the average short-term rate investors expect over the next ten years, plus a term premium: extra pay for locking money up through unknown inflation, government deficits and a flood of new bonds. When inflation expectations rise or the government borrows heavily, buyers demand more, bond prices fall and yields climb.
Lending for ten years is a bet on a decade of inflation and policy. When that future looks less certain, lenders want to be paid for the risk.
The Fed steers the short end of the curve; markets set the long end. Mortgages, corporate loans and stock valuations follow the long end.
What are inflation expectations doing right now?
Is government borrowing rising?
Do I need fixed-rate debt now, or can I wait?

title: Crack spreads: why diesel can soar faster than oil
layers: Nobody puts crude oil in a truck. Crude has to be refined into products like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, and each product has its own price set by its own supply and demand. The gap between what a refinery pays for crude and what it earns selling the products is called the crack spread, because refining 'cracks' heavy oil molecules into lighter fuels. When that gap blows out, fuel prices can climb much faster than oil.

The US Energy Information Administration uses a simple model called the 3:2:1 crack spread: three barrels of crude yield roughly two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of diesel. Add the wholesale price of the two barrels of gasoline and the one of diesel (fuel is quoted per gallon, so multiply by 42 gallons per barrel), subtract the cost of three barrels of crude, and divide by three. The result is a rough profit per barrel before the refinery's other costs. Analysts also track single-product spreads. Example with made-up round numbers: if crude costs $90 a barrel and diesel sells wholesale for $4.50 a gallon, a barrel of diesel is worth $189, so the diesel crack is $99. In August 2026 the real US diesel crack passed $100 a barrel for the first time. The spread widens when refining capacity, not oil, is the bottleneck: refineries knocked out by attacks or hurricanes, plants already running flat out (US refineries hit 98% utilization in late August 2026), low inventories, or a seasonal jump in demand. Diesel demand rises in autumn with harvest and trucking (US distillate use rises about 4% from September to October on average) and then winter heating oil, while gasoline enters its slow season. That is why diesel can set records while gasoline barely moves.

Refineries are huge, slow to build and few in number, so a fuel shortage cannot be fixed by pumping more crude. In 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted one of the world's biggest diesel exporters, US diesel hit a weekly high of $5.81 a gallon. In 2026 the same thing is happening for a different mix of reasons: attacks on Russian refineries cut its diesel output about 30%, and the Iran war choked flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Diesel matters more to the economy than gasoline because it moves freight, food and machinery, so a diesel squeeze spreads into prices of almost everything that gets shipped. Wide crack spreads move money too: they are a windfall for refiners and a cost for airlines, truckers, farmers and retailers.

Oil is the raw material, but the price you and your suppliers pay is set at the refinery. When product prices rise faster than crude, the problem is refining capacity, and it usually takes longer to fix than a crude shortage.
Is the price jump in crude itself, or in refined products like diesel?
Who in my supply chain pays for fuel, and how quickly do they pass it on to me?
What would ease the bottleneck: new refining capacity, restored exports, or the end of a seasonal peak?

title: Cyclical industries: when record profits are a warning
layers: A cyclical industry is one where profits rise and fall in big waves, because prices swing with the balance of supply and demand rather than with anything the company controls. Memory chips, oil, steel, shipping, airlines, chemicals and homebuilding all behave this way. What they share: the product is close to a commodity (one maker's chip or barrel is nearly interchangeable with another's), buyers shop on price, and new capacity is expensive and takes years to build. Micron, one of three big memory makers, shows the pattern. In fiscal 2022 it earned $8.7 billion. In fiscal 2023 revenue fell 49% and it lost $5.8 billion, with a gross margin of minus 9.1%, meaning it sold chips for less than they cost to make. By mid-2026 its adjusted gross margin had reached 87%.

The cycle runs like a loop. Demand jumps (in 2026, AI data centers need huge amounts of memory) while supply is fixed, so prices soar. Soaring prices create fat profits, and every producer uses them to build new factories. Factories take two to three years to come online, so they tend to arrive together, often just as demand cools. Now supply outruns demand, buyers stop ordering and burn through their stockpiles, and prices fall fast because a factory that has already been built is cheapest to keep running, even at a thin margin. That is what happened in early 2023: Micron's DRAM prices dropped about 20% in a single quarter, revenue fell 53% from a year earlier, it wrote down $1.43 billion of inventory and planned to cut close to 15% of its workforce. Losses then force producers to cut investment, supply tightens, and the next boom starts. A second force is technology. A cheaper way to make the same product, like a denser chip design that fits more memory in the same space, works like new supply even before a new factory opens, because it lowers what each unit costs to produce.

Cyclicals trick investors in a specific way. The price-to-earnings ratio (share price divided by profit per share) usually signals 'cheap' when it is low. For a cyclical company at the top of the cycle, profits are temporarily huge, so the P/E looks low exactly when the risk is highest. At the bottom, profits are tiny or negative, so the P/E looks high or meaningless just when the outlook is about to improve. Professional investors handle this by looking at 'normalized' or 'mid-cycle' earnings, an average across a full boom and bust, and by watching supply rather than demand: how much capacity competitors are building, how full customer inventories are, and whether a new low-cost producer is entering. Markets also move ahead of profits. On October 12–13, 2026, memory stocks fell sharply on news that China's CXMT might make denser chips, even though prices were still rising and the threat was not yet in production. Micron's own earlier cycle shows how fast profits fade: from a $14.1 billion peak in fiscal 2018, net income fell 81% in two years.

In a commodity business, the most dangerous moment is when everyone is earning record profits, because those profits fund the new supply that ends them. Judge a cyclical company by its earnings across a full cycle, and watch the supply side more closely than the demand story.
Is this company's product easy to swap for a competitor's, so that price decides who wins?
Are today's profits far above the company's average over the last full cycle?
How much new capacity are competitors building, and when does it come online?
If prices fell 20% in a quarter, could this company still cover its costs and debts?

title: Inside the inflation number: headline, core and the basket
layers: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a monthly measure of how much a fixed basket of goods and services costs compared with before. The Bureau of Labor Statistics collects prices across the economy, from rent and gasoline to airfares and haircuts, and groups them into categories. Each category gets a weight called its relative importance, based on how much households actually spend on it. In August 2026 shelter was 35.3% of the basket, food 13.5%, energy 7.4% and gasoline alone 3.9%. 'Headline' inflation is the change in the whole basket. 'Core' inflation strips out food and energy, which together are about 21% of the basket, leaving the other 79%. The number in the news is usually the change over 12 months.

A category's effect on the total is roughly its weight times its price change. In September 2026 gasoline rose 9.1% in one month. Multiply by its 3.9% weight and you get about 0.35 percentage points, which is why the BLS said gasoline accounted for over half of the 0.6% monthly rise in all prices. Over 12 months gasoline was up 34.2% and energy 20.4%, while core rose only 2.6%. That gap, 3.7% headline against 2.6% core, is the whole story of that report: an energy shock sitting on top of a much calmer underlying trend. Housing works differently. Most people own their home, so the BLS does not use house prices. It asks what an owned home would rent for, a measure called owners' equivalent rent (25.9% of the basket on its own), and estimates changes from a sample of rented homes. Each home in the sample is priced only every six months, and it reflects what tenants are paying now, including on old leases. So shelter moves slowly and keeps reporting yesterday's rent changes for a long time after new-lease rents turn. Monthly figures are adjusted for seasonal patterns; the 12-month figures are not.

Central banks care most about the part of inflation that sticks. Food and energy prices can jump on a war, a hurricane or a bad harvest and then fall back, and interest rates can do nothing to make more oil. Core is a better guide to where inflation will settle, so policymakers watch it closely. The Federal Reserve's official 2% target is set on a different measure, the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE), so the CPI and the Fed's own gauge can tell slightly different stories. The danger is when an energy shock leaks into everything else: transport and airfares cost more, companies raise prices, workers ask for higher pay, and people start expecting inflation to stay high. In September 2026, airfares were up 22.4% over the year, a sign that fuel costs were already spreading. Bond markets react to surprises: when core came in 0.1 point above forecast, the 10-year Treasury yield rose more than 6 basis points that morning as investors priced in the chance of another Fed hike.

Read every inflation report in three steps. First, compare headline with core to see whether the rise is broad or concentrated in energy and food. Second, look at the biggest weights, shelter above all, because a small move there outweighs a big move in a small category. Third, compare the result with what economists expected, because markets move on the surprise. Then translate it into your life: your personal inflation rate depends on your own basket. A household that drives a lot and rents feels this report far more than one that works from home and owns with a fixed mortgage. Any cash or bond earning less than inflation is losing purchasing power, even if its balance grows.
Is this rise broad, or mostly energy and food?
Is core inflation speeding up or slowing down over the last three months?
What would my own inflation rate be, given how I spend?
Is my cash earning more than inflation after tax?

title: Natural gas and LNG: why the world has no single gas price
layers: Natural gas heats homes, runs power plants, and is the raw material for fertilizer and many chemicals. Unlike oil, it has no single world price. It trades in regional markets with their own benchmarks: Henry Hub in the US, TTF in Europe (traded in euros per megawatt-hour), and JKM for spot cargoes into Japan and Korea. The same molecule can cost several times more in Rotterdam or Tokyo than in Louisiana. In October 2026, Europe's TTF reached about €86, roughly 160% above a year earlier, while its all-time high was €345 in March 2022.

Gas is a gas, so it is bulky and expensive to move. On land it travels by pipeline, which ties buyer and seller together for decades. To cross oceans it must be liquefied: the US Energy Information Administration explains that cooling gas to about -260°F shrinks it about 600 times. Special tankers carry it in cryogenic tanks, and an import terminal turns it back into gas. Each step, liquefaction plants, ships and regasification terminals, costs billions and takes years to build, so supply cannot respond quickly when prices jump. The price gap between regions is what pays for that chain. A US exporter with flexible cargoes sends them wherever the price after shipping is highest, which is why traders watch the spread between TTF and JKM: when Asia pays more, cargoes head east and Europe has to raise its bid. Storage adds a seasonal rhythm. Europe fills underground tanks over summer and draws them down in winter, so a low fill level in October means buyers must compete hard for cargoes all winter.

It matters far beyond the gas bill. In Europe's power markets, the most expensive plant needed to meet demand often sets the price for all electricity, and that plant is frequently gas-fired, so a gas spike lifts power prices across the board. Fertilizer makers use gas as their main input, so expensive gas feeds into food prices a season later. Energy-heavy industries such as chemicals, steel and glass lose money or shut lines, which is why EU industrial gas demand in September 2026 was nearly 30% below pre-2022 levels in Citi's sample. Geography is destiny here: Persian Gulf supply is about 20% of global LNG exports and passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so one chokepoint can reprice energy for a continent. The 2022 crisis taught the same lesson after Russian pipeline gas stopped flowing to most of Europe.

Energy is a cost hiding inside almost every business and every price you pay. When you read that gas is up, ask which region, because a European chemical company and an American one can face opposite fortunes from the same headline. Cheap local gas is a competitive advantage that can last years, and the long build times of LNG plants mean shortages and gluts both last longer than people expect. Volatile commodities punish anyone who assumes today's price is permanent, whether they are budgeting a household, pricing a product or valuing a company.
Which regional gas price, Henry Hub, TTF or JKM, actually drives the costs of this company or my utility bill?
How much of this business's cost base is energy, and can it pass higher costs on to customers?
Is today's price driven by a temporary disruption or by a long-term shortage of supply capacity?
How full is storage compared with normal, and what happens if the winter is colder than expected?

title: Cost of capital: the hurdle every investment has to clear
layers: Every dollar a company spends came from someone who expects to be paid back: lenders want interest, and shareholders want a return that beats what they could earn elsewhere for the same risk. The blended price of that money is the cost of capital. A project creates value only when it earns more than this cost. Growth alone proves nothing; a company can double its sales and still make its owners poorer.

Finance teams estimate it as the weighted average cost of capital, or WACC. Take the cost of debt (the yield lenders demand today, reduced by the tax deduction on interest) and the cost of equity (a risk-free rate such as the 10-year Treasury, plus a premium for how risky the business is), then weight each by how much of the company it funds. Then compare it with return on invested capital, ROIC: operating profit after tax divided by all the money tied up in the business. A simple illustration: a company earning 12% on its data centers creates value if its capital costs 9%, and destroys value on every new building if its capital costs 15%. The buildings and the customers are the same; only the price of money changed. That is why CoreWeave's bonds matter. Its 9.625% notes due 2032 yielded above 15% in October 2026, its second-quarter interest expense of $640 million was nearly a quarter of revenue, and it carried about $35.6 billion of debt principal. Lenders are telling the company its next dollar will cost far more than its last.

Debt is cheaper than equity because lenders are paid first and interest is tax-deductible, so borrowing can raise returns for owners. But debt has a deadline. When rates rise or lenders get nervous, maturing loans must be refinanced at the new, higher price, and the hurdle rises for the whole business. Collateral matters too: if lenders believe chips wear out in three or four years while the company depreciates them over longer, they will price that gap into the yield. Equity investors feel it last and most, because they are paid only after every lender.

Judge a company, or your own business, by the spread between what its capital earns and what its capital costs, and watch whether that spread is widening or shrinking. The bond market often sees a shrinking spread before the stock market does.
Does this business earn more on its capital than its capital costs, and by how much?
How much debt comes due in the next two years, and at what rate could it be refinanced today?
Is interest expense growing faster than revenue?
If I borrow to grow my own business, what return does each new dollar need to clear?

title: Sales and trading: how banks profit when markets move
layers: Every time a pension fund sells a block of shares, a hedge fund borrows to bet on a stock, or a company swaps euros for dollars, a bank's trading desk is usually on the other side. Sales and trading is the business of standing in the middle of those trades. It is split into two big desks: equities (stocks and stock derivatives) and FICC, which stands for fixed income, currencies and commodities (bonds, interest-rate products, currencies, oil and metals). At the largest banks it is one of the biggest sources of revenue, and it is the most volatile one.

Desks earn money in two main ways. The first is intermediation, also called market making: the bank quotes a price to buy (the bid) and a slightly higher price to sell (the ask) and keeps the gap, the bid-ask spread. To do this it must hold inventory, so it carries the risk that prices move against it before it can offload a position. It earns more when clients trade more, which usually happens when markets are jumpy. The second is financing: lending cash or securities to clients. Prime brokerage gives hedge funds margin loans to buy more than their own money allows, lends them shares to sell short, and earns interest and fees on the balances. Repo desks lend cash against bonds as collateral. Financing behaves more like a loan book than a bet, but it grows with the amount of leverage in the system. Goldman's third quarter of 2026 shows both engines: equities revenue of $6.44 billion, with $3.08 billion from intermediation (up 52%) and $3.37 billion from financing (up 96%). Its FICC revenue was $3.47 billion, about flat, because weaker credit, mortgage and rate trading offset growth in FICC financing. Since the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, the Volcker rule limits big US banks from making pure bets with their own money, so most trading profit is supposed to come from serving clients rather than speculating.

Investors judge revenue by its quality, not just its size. Net interest income from loans and management fees on client assets tend to repeat quarter after quarter. Trading revenue depends on volatility, client activity and appetite for borrowing, so a record quarter can be followed by a sharp drop. For that reason the market typically values a bank built on fees and deposits at a higher multiple of earnings than one that depends on trading. Costs matter too: traders are paid largely in bonuses, so pay rises with revenue. Goldman's operating expenses rose 20% in the quarter as revenue rose 23%. Analysts track the efficiency ratio, costs divided by revenue; Goldman's was 59.4% for the first nine months of 2026, versus 62.1% a year earlier, meaning it kept more of each dollar earned. Trading booms also say something about the wider market: when financing to hedge funds is the fastest-growing line, more borrowed money is chasing assets, which raises the risk of forced selling if prices fall.

Split every set of results into the parts that repeat and the parts that depend on markets, then decide how much each is worth. A bank, an asset manager or any company with a trading arm can look strongest at the peak of a cycle, exactly when its most volatile income is at its highest. Read the segment table, not only the headline profit.
What share of this company's revenue would still be there in a calm, quiet market?
Is the growth coming from more clients and fees, or from more volatility and more leverage?
How much of the extra revenue is going straight out again as pay and other costs?
If markets fell sharply, which lines would shrink first, and which could turn into losses?

title: Sovereign debt: when a country's borrowing becomes the risk
layers: Governments borrow by selling bonds, and the interest rate investors demand on that debt is the base price of money in that country. Banks, companies and home buyers all borrow at that base plus a margin, so when a government's cost of borrowing rises, everyone's does. The cleanest way to see how much risk investors attach to a government is its spread: the extra yield it pays over a borrower seen as the safest in the same currency. In the euro area that benchmark is Germany. France paying 4.79% for ten years while Germany pays 3.42% means investors want 1.37 percentage points more each year to hold French debt, even though both are paid back in the same euros.

Whether a government's debt is sustainable comes down to four numbers: how much it owes compared with the size of its economy (debt-to-GDP), the average interest rate on that debt (r), how fast the economy grows in money terms (g), and the primary balance, meaning taxes minus spending before interest. If r is below g, a country can carry a lot of debt and the ratio shrinks on its own as the economy outgrows it. If r rises above g, the debt ratio climbs every year unless the government runs a primary surplus to offset it. A simple example: with debt at 120% of GDP, every 1 point rise in the average interest rate eventually adds about 1.2% of GDP to the yearly interest bill. That happens slowly, because old bonds only reprice as they mature. France's tradable debt has an average life of about eight and a half years, which is why a rate shock shows up as a steady squeeze rather than an overnight bill. Credit rating agencies such as Moody's, S&P and Fitch read these same numbers plus politics, and a downgrade can force some funds that are only allowed to hold top-rated debt to sell.

Countries that print their own currency, like the US, the UK or Japan, can always pay in that currency, so their risk tends to show up as inflation or a weaker currency instead of default. Euro countries gave that up: the European Central Bank sets one policy for 21 countries, but each one writes its own budget. That makes a French or Italian bond closer to a corporate bond than a US Treasury, because the government cannot create the euros it owes. This is what turned 2010 to 2012 into a crisis. Spain's spread over Germany sat near zero from 2002 to 2007, then rose above 5 percentage points. Higher rates made deficits bigger, which pushed rates higher again, and banks holding their own government's bonds weakened together with it. The spiral broke on July 26, 2012, when ECB President Mario Draghi said the bank would do 'whatever it takes to preserve the euro.' Today the ECB has a tool to cap unjustified spreads, but its rules exclude countries already in breach of EU deficit rules, which includes France, so markets cannot assume the same safety net.

A government bond is only risk-free if the government controls the currency it borrows in and the politics allow it to raise taxes or cut spending when needed. Watch three things: whether interest rates on the debt are rising faster than the economy is growing, whether the government can pass a budget at all, and how much of the debt is held by foreigners who can leave quickly. About 60% of French government debt is held abroad. When a spread widens, it moves the price of everything built on top of that bond, from bank shares to mortgages to the currency.
What share of my bond fund is in government debt, and from which countries?
Is this country's interest bill growing faster than its economy?
Does this government borrow in a currency it controls?
If this bond were downgraded, who would be forced to sell it?

title: Index providers: the rulebook behind your index fund
layers: An index is a list of companies chosen by written rules, plus a formula for how much of each to hold. A handful of companies write most of these rulebooks: S&P Dow Jones Indices, MSCI, FTSE Russell and a few others. An index fund does not choose stocks. It copies the list. So when you buy a 'total market' or 'world' fund, you are really buying a set of decisions made by an index committee and its methodology documents. By the end of 2023, passive US mutual funds and ETFs held about $13.3 trillion, slightly more than active funds for the first time, according to Morningstar data reported by the Financial Times. That means the rulebook now steers more money than stock pickers do.

Every index answers four questions. First, the universe: which countries, exchanges and share types count. Second, eligibility: what a company must be to get in, such as a minimum size, enough shares that trade freely (the 'free float'), enough daily trading, and for some indexes, profitability. MSCI's new rule for 'non-operating' companies is an eligibility test: it asks whether a company runs a business or mostly holds investments, like a fund does. Third, weighting: most big indexes weight by market value adjusted for free float, so the largest companies get the most money. Fourth, maintenance: indexes are reviewed on a schedule, usually quarterly, and changes are announced ahead of an effective date. Rules include 'buffers' so companies near a cutoff do not bounce in and out every review. MSCI, for example, removes a current member only if it fails its new screen in two straight annual filings, which cuts trading costs for funds.

Rule changes matter because index funds must trade on the effective date, no matter the price. When a company joins, funds tracking that index must buy; when it leaves, they must sell. Strategy says funds tracking MSCI's global indexes hold about 13 million of its shares, about 3.1% of its basic shares, which would have to be sold if it is removed. Traders know this, so they try to buy before inclusions and sell before removals. That front-running has largely competed the old 'index effect' away. An S&P study found that stocks added to the S&P 500 earned a median 8.32% above the market between announcement and inclusion in 1995-1999, but about zero (-0.04%) in 2011-2021. Index changes still shift ownership and trading, but the price jump is no longer a free lunch. Rules also shape what you own in subtler ways: a market-value weighting means a world fund holds more of whatever has already risen most, and an eligibility rule can quietly keep a whole category, such as companies that are mostly bitcoin holdings, out of your portfolio.

An index fund is passive about trading, not about choices. Someone chose the universe, the entry rules and the weights, and those choices decide your risk, your sector mix and your country exposure. Two 'world' funds from different providers can hold different companies in different amounts. Before you rely on a fund, read the one-page summary of the index it tracks: what is included, how it is weighted, how often it changes. Then judge the fund on cost and on how closely it tracks the index, and judge the index on whether its rules match what you want to own.
Which index does my fund track, and who writes its rules?
What must a company be to get in, and what gets it removed?
Is the index weighted by market value, equally, or by something else, and how concentrated does that make my fund?
How often is the index reviewed, and does a rule change I read about affect anything I own?

title: New homes vs resale: builders, rate buydowns and the lock-in effect
layers: The US housing market is really two markets. The resale market is millions of households selling homes they already live in; the new-home market is a few hundred builders selling homes they built as a business. They respond to the same mortgage rates in opposite ways. A homeowner can simply refuse to sell. A builder cannot: it has borrowed to buy land and pay for construction, and every unsold house costs interest, taxes and upkeep each month. So when rates jump, resale supply dries up while builders keep selling, and builders become the part of the market where prices and deals move first. The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index measures how builders feel: it surveys them on current sales, sales expected over the next six months, and buyer traffic, and anything below 50 means more builders call conditions poor than good. In October 2026 it fell to 29, its lowest since June 2012, with buyer traffic at 18.

Two mechanisms drive this. The first is the lock-in effect. Most US homeowners have a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, so a family that borrowed at 3% keeps that rate only if it stays put; moving means taking a new loan at today's rate. An FHFA study found that for every percentage point market rates sit above a borrower's own rate, the chance they sell falls by 18.1%, and that lock-in prevented about 1.33 million home sales between mid-2022 and the end of 2023. Fewer resales mean fewer homes for buyers to choose from, which pushed prices up an estimated 5.7%, more than the 3.3% that higher rates pushed them down. The second mechanism is how builders compete for the buyers left over: incentives. The most powerful is a rate buydown, where the builder pays the lender up front to lower the buyer's rate. Paying down a rate for the whole loan costs roughly 1% of the loan amount for each 0.25 point of rate, according to John Burns Research and Consulting, so cutting a rate from 6.5% to 5.0% can take 5-6% of the purchase price. A cheaper version, the 2-1 buydown, lowers the rate by two points in year one and one point in year two, costs about 2% of the price, but still requires the buyer to qualify at the full rate.

Builders often prefer buydowns and other incentives to cutting the list price, for business reasons. A lower list price becomes a public comparable sale that drags down appraisals on every other home in the community and signals weakness to buyers who already signed contracts, who may cancel. A buydown moves the buyer's monthly payment, which is what most buyers can actually afford, while keeping the recorded price higher. That is why, in October 2026, 65% of builders offered incentives, the 19th straight month at or above 60%, even as 43% also cut prices by an average of 6%. When both levers are being pulled at once, the builder's gross margin is being squeezed from two sides. This is also why builder surveys are a leading indicator. Buyer traffic falls before signed contracts, contracts fall before construction starts, and starts drive jobs in construction, lumber, appliances and furniture. Housing has historically turned down before the wider economy, so economists watch builder sentiment closely. Big public builders with cheap land bought years ago and their own mortgage arms can absorb buydowns; small builders who rely on costly construction loans cannot, so slumps tend to shift market share to the largest companies.

Price is not the same as cost. In a slow market, the real price of a new home is the list price minus any rate buydown, closing-cost help and upgrades, and the rate buydown can be worth tens of thousands of dollars over the loan. Compare offers on monthly payment and total cost, not sticker price, and check whether a buydown is permanent or temporary. On the economy side, read builder confidence and buyer traffic as early signals: they tend to move before housing starts, jobs and prices do. And remember that a market with few resales and heavy builder discounting is not one market in balance; it is two markets reacting differently to the same rates.
If a builder offers either a price cut or a rate buydown of the same dollar value, which one lowers my monthly payment more, and which one helps more if I refinance or sell in a few years?
Is this buydown permanent for the life of the loan, or temporary, and will I qualify at the full rate?
How does my current mortgage rate compare with today's rate, and what would moving actually cost me each month?
Are builder confidence and buyer traffic rising or falling, and what does that suggest for housing jobs and prices over the next year?

title: Priced in: how markets put odds on the Fed's next move
layers: Eight times a year the Federal Reserve's committee sets a target range for the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. That one rate anchors what you earn on savings and what you pay on credit cards, car loans and, indirectly, mortgages. Long before each meeting, markets publish a running estimate of what the Fed will do: when you read that traders see an 88% chance of a hike, that number comes from 30-day fed funds futures traded on the CME, and CME's FedWatch tool turns their prices into probabilities. It is not a poll of economists or of the Fed. It is a price: what traders with money at stake are willing to pay right now.

Each futures contract covers one calendar month and trades at 100 minus the average fed funds rate the market expects for that month. A contract at 95.67 implies an average rate of 4.33%; a 2015 December contract at 99.78 implied 0.22%. To turn a price into odds, compare the implied rate with today's rate. A simplified example with made-up numbers: suppose the effective rate is 3.88% and a contract for a month after the meeting trades at 95.93, implying 4.07%. That is 0.19 points above today. A full hike is 0.25 points, so the market is pricing 0.19 / 0.25, about 76% of a hike, which reads as roughly a 76% chance of a hike and 24% of no change. Real calculations are messier: a meeting in mid-month means the month's average mixes the old rate and the new one, so the tool has to back out the post-meeting rate, and it chains months together to estimate later meetings. In 2015 Bloomberg and CME read the same contracts as 74% and 73.6% odds, and the Financial Times argued both understated how sure traders really were, because of where they assumed the effective rate would settle inside the new range.

The odds move fast because prices move fast. In September 2026, comments on inflation from Fed official Christopher Waller cut the odds of a September hike from around 67% to about 54.6% within minutes, according to investingLive: traders changed what they would pay for a contract, and the probability followed. This is why the phrase 'already priced in' matters. Bond yields, mortgage rates, the dollar and assets with no yield such as gold adjust to the expected path of rates as soon as the odds shift. When the Fed then does exactly what was priced, markets often barely react. What moves prices on decision day is the surprise: the gap between what happened and what the futures had built in, plus any change in the Fed's signal about the meetings after.

Read rate odds as a snapshot of positioning, not a forecast. A 50% reading does not mean the Fed is flipping a coin; it means traders are split and the next data point can swing them sharply. Odds far out in time are less reliable than odds for the next meeting, and they can embed a small risk premium rather than pure expectation. Use them for one practical job: before you lock in a CD, choose a fixed or variable loan, or pick a bond fund's duration, check what the market already expects. You are only rewarded or hurt by the part of the future that is not yet in the price.
What does the futures market already expect the Fed to do at its next two meetings, and how much has that changed in the past week?
If the Fed does exactly what is priced, which of my rates will actually change, and which have already moved?
What news, such as an inflation report or oil shock, could push the odds sharply the other way?
Am I treating a market probability as a forecast, or as the current price of an uncertain outcome?

title: Share classes: owning a company without a vote
layers: A share normally bundles two things: a claim on the company's profits and a vote on who runs it. A multi-class structure pulls those apart. One class may carry ten votes per share and sit with the founders, another carries one vote and trades publicly, and a third may carry no vote at all. Every class usually has the same claim on dividends and on the company's value, so the price of each class tracks closely, but control does not follow the money. Meta's new Class C stock, approved in October 2026, is a pure economic claim: it trades on Nasdaq but carries no vote.

Companies create a new class in one of two ways. The first is at the IPO, when founders keep high-vote shares and sell low-vote shares to the public. The second is a stock dividend: every holder receives one new nonvoting share for each share they own, which works like a two-for-one stock split. Meta is doing the second, giving one Class C share per Class A and Class B share, and says the market price of Class A should then reflect the effect of a two-for-one split. Nobody's voting power changes on day one. The power shows up later: once the nonvoting class exists, the company can sell it for cash, pay employees with it, or use it to buy other companies, and none of those new shares dilute the founder's vote. Alphabet used the same move in 2014, which kept Larry Page and Sergey Brin's combined control just over 50%, and this year half of its $85 billion of new stock for AI carried no vote.

Founders argue that control lets them make long, expensive bets that quarterly-minded shareholders would block. Meta points to stock growth of more than 1,700% since its IPO versus about 495% for the S&P 500. Critics answer that control without accountability removes the main check on a CEO: shareholders cannot replace the board if a bet goes wrong. The timing matters too. Meta's Q3 2026 capital spending of $34.9 billion pushed free cash flow to negative $2.12 billion, and when a company spends more than it earns, it has to borrow or sell shares. Nonvoting stock makes selling shares easier politically, which also makes dilution easier. Meta tried a similar class in 2017 and dropped it after investor pushback, according to Semafor, so this time it secured approval by written consent of holders who control the vote.

Separate the money from the control and evaluate each. The economic question is the same for any share: is the company earning more on new capital than that capital costs, and how fast is the share count growing? The control question is who can fire management if they are wrong, and the answer in a founder-controlled company is often no one. Before buying into a company directly or judging one you hold through a fund, find the share classes and votes per share in the annual report or proxy, check who controls the majority of votes, and track the share count over several years. A rising share count with falling free cash flow is the pattern that matters, whatever the voting rights.
How many votes does each share class carry, and who controls the majority of the vote?
Is the share count rising, and what is the new stock being used for: cash, employee pay or acquisitions?
If management's big bet fails, what mechanism, if any, lets shareholders change course?
Does free cash flow cover the company's spending, or does it depend on selling shares or borrowing?

title: Bear markets: the math of falling and getting back
layers: A bear market is a fall of 20% or more from a market's most recent peak. A correction is a smaller fall of 10% to 20%, and a bull market is the rise that follows a low. The line at 20% is a convention, not a law, but it is the one the financial press and data providers use. By Ned Davis Research's count, cited by Hartford Funds, the S&P 500 has had 27 bear markets since 1928. The average one cut prices by about 35% and lasted 289 days, roughly 9.6 months. The average bull market gained 112% and lasted 988 days, about 2.7 years. In October 2026, China's CSI 300 crossed the line, closing 20.2% below its June peak.

The key mechanic is that losses and gains are not symmetric. Recovery takes a bigger percentage gain than the loss, because the gain starts from a smaller base. The formula is: gain needed = 1 / (1 - loss) - 1. A 20% fall needs a 25% gain to break even. A 35% fall, the historical average, needs about 54%. A 50% fall needs 100%. Time and depth together decide how long you are underwater. Japan is the extreme case: the Nikkei 225 peaked at 38,915.87 on December 29, 1989, then fell below 8,200 in 2011, a loss of more than 78%, after banks wrote off about 100 trillion yen of bad debts. Getting back needed a gain of more than 375%. The index finally closed above its old record on February 22, 2024, more than 34 years later. Most bear markets end far faster, but Japan shows what happens when a market starts from bubble prices.

Bear markets happen for a few recurring reasons: prices ran ahead of profits, interest rates rose and made safer assets more attractive, a recession cut earnings, or a shock like a war or financial crisis. They do not always mean recession. There have been 27 bear markets since 1928 but only 15 recessions, according to Hartford Funds. China in 2026 shows the gap: the economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter while stocks fell 20%, because investors had paid high prices for tech and AI profits that came in weaker than hoped. The behavior side matters as much as the math. About 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days in the last 20 years came during bear markets, and another 36% came in the first two months of a new bull market, before it was obvious one had begun. Selling after a fall locks in the loss and risks missing the days that drive the recovery.

You cannot predict bear markets, so plan for them. Over a 50-year investing life, expect to live through about 14. That means three things. First, keep money you need within a few years in cash or short-term bonds, so a fall never forces you to sell stocks at the bottom. Second, diversify across countries and asset types, because a single market can stay down for decades, as Japan's did. Third, judge risk by drawdown, not by average return: ask how deep a fall your portfolio could take and whether you could hold through it. Rebalancing into a falling asset feels wrong but is how disciplined investors buy low by rule rather than by nerve.
How far is this market from its last peak, and what gain would it need to get back to even?
Is the fall driven by lower profits, higher interest rates, or investors paying less for the same profits?
How much of my portfolio sits in this one market or sector, and could I hold it through a 35% or 50% drop?
Do I have enough cash set aside that I would never be forced to sell during a fall?

title: Inflation expectations: when believing in higher prices makes them happen
layers: Inflation expectations are the rate at which households, businesses and investors think prices will rise. They are measured two ways. Surveys ask people directly: the University of Michigan polls about 600 households a month on prices over the next year and over the next 5 to 10 years, and the New York Fed and professional forecasters run their own. Markets give a second reading: the 10-year breakeven rate is the yield on an ordinary 10-year Treasury minus the yield on a 10-year TIPS, the inflation-protected version. The gap is roughly the inflation investors need to be paid for, though it also carries a risk premium. The Fed even blends 21 measures into one index.

Expectations turn into real prices through contracts and decisions. If workers expect 3% inflation, they ask for at least 3% raises just to stand still. If a business expects its wages, rent and suppliers to cost 3% more, it raises its own prices ahead of time. Those higher wages and prices then show up in the official data, which confirms the original belief and pushes the next round of expectations higher. That loop is the wage-price spiral, and once it starts it can keep inflation high even when unemployment rises, which is what happened in the 1970s. Brookings estimates that, all else equal, a one point rise in expectations tends to lift actual inflation by about one point. The loop also runs in reverse: if people expect falling prices, they delay purchases, which is why central banks fear deflation too.

This is why the Fed watches expectations as closely as inflation itself. Economists call expectations anchored when a burst of high prices barely moves what people expect over the long run; Ben Bernanke defined it as being relatively insensitive to incoming data. Anchored expectations give the Fed room to look through a temporary shock like an oil spike. Unanchored ones force it to act harshly. In June 2022, when Michigan's 1-year reading hit 5.3% and the long-run reading jumped, the Fed raised rates by 0.75 point, its biggest single move since 1994, and Powell named rising expectations as a reason. Two details help you read the numbers: consumers have historically expected more inflation than actually arrived, so the trend matters more than the level, and the 5-to-10-year figure matters more than the 1-year one, because short-term views swing with gas prices while long-term views reveal whether people still trust the 2% target.

Treat long-run inflation expectations as a gauge of trust in the central bank. When the 1-year number jumps on an energy shock but the long-run number holds, the Fed can be patient and rate cuts stay possible. When the long-run number climbs, expect rates to stay higher for longer, with costlier mortgages and loans, pressure on bond prices and on the valuations of companies whose profits are far in the future. In your own business, expectations are also a negotiating fact: they shape what employees will ask for, what customers will tolerate, and how long you should lock in supplier prices or fixed-rate debt.
Is the long-run (5 to 10 year) expectation moving, or only the 1-year number?
Do survey measures and the market breakeven rate tell the same story?
Is the jump driven by a temporary shock like oil, or by broad price and wage increases?
If expectations stay high, which of my costs, prices and loans reset first?

title: The carry trade: borrowing where money is cheap
layers: A carry trade borrows money in a currency with low interest rates and invests it in a currency or asset that pays more. The profit is the carry: the gap between what you earn and what you pay to borrow. The classic funding currency is the Japanese yen, because the Bank of Japan kept its rates at or near zero for years. The Swiss franc has played the same role. The money then flows into US Treasuries, US stocks, or high-rate currencies like the Mexican peso. The Bank for International Settlements put a rough middle estimate of yen-funded carry trades at about ¥40 trillion, or $250 billion, going into August 2024, and said that figure was probably too low.

Say a fund borrows yen at 0.1% and swaps it into dollars to buy a Treasury yielding 5%. If the exchange rate stays still, it earns close to 4.9 points a year, and with borrowed money stacked on top, say five times its own capital, the return on its own money is far larger. The catch is that the trade has two moving parts. Economic theory, called uncovered interest parity, says a high-rate currency should fall over time by about the rate gap, wiping out the gain. In practice it often does not, for years at a time, which is why the trade is popular. But when the funding currency jumps, the losses arrive all at once: a 10% rise in the yen erases two years of a 5-point carry, and with leverage it can wipe out the fund. Lenders then raise margin requirements, so traders must sell whatever they own, stocks, bonds, other currencies, to repay yen, which pushes the yen up further. The BIS calls this procyclical deleveraging: selling that feeds on itself.

That is what happened in August 2024. The BoJ raised its rate to 0.25% at the end of July, a weak US economic report days later stoked recession fears and bets on Fed cuts, and the rate gap that carry traders lived on suddenly looked set to shrink. The yen surged, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 12.4% on August 5 and the Mexican peso fell more than 6% in the upheaval. Markets bounced within days, but the episode showed that a currency trade can move stock prices worldwide. Carry trades funded in yen and Swiss francs also played a part in Iceland's financial meltdown in 2007 and 2008. Now the BoJ is at 1.25% and talking about more, so the cheapest funding source in the world is no longer cheap, while US 10-year yields near 5% keep the gap wide enough to tempt borrowers.

Read a carry trade as picking up coins in front of a steamroller: small, steady gains most of the time, then a sudden large loss when the funding currency turns. The warning signs are a narrowing rate gap, a sharply rising funding currency, and spikes in market volatility, because each one forces leveraged traders to sell at the same time. For you, this explains why a central bank decision in Tokyo can knock your US index fund, and why currency moves can add to or subtract from the returns on any foreign investment you hold. It applies to your own borrowing too: a loan in a currency you do not earn in is a carry trade, and a jump in that currency raises what you owe.
What is the interest rate gap between the two currencies, and is it likely to widen or shrink from here?
How much is borrowed against this position, and what happens if lenders ask for more collateral?
If the funding currency rose 10% in a month, how many years of carry would that erase?
Do I earn in the same currency I owe, or am I making a currency bet without meaning to?

title: The deposit franchise: why idle cash is a bank's best asset
layers: A bank's deposit franchise is the value of its customers' cash that stays put even when the bank pays far less than the market rate. Checking accounts are the core of it: Apollo's Torsten Slok puts the average checking rate near 0.1%, while savings products elsewhere pay 3.3% to 5%. Customers accept that gap because moving money is a chore, because direct deposit, bill pay and cards are wired to one account, and because the account comes with payment services and access to cash. Deposits make up roughly 80% of US bank liabilities, according to the New York Fed, so how cheaply a bank can keep them decides much of what it earns.

Analysts measure stickiness with the deposit beta: how much of a change in market rates a bank passes on to depositors. If the Fed raises rates by 4 points and a bank lifts its savings rate by 1 point, its beta is 25%. A beta of zero means deposits behave like fixed-rate funding that never reprices; a beta of one means the bank pays the market rate in full and the franchise is worth nothing. The New York Fed notes that deposit betas have stayed below one for the past thirty years, which is why banks profit when rates rise: their loans and securities reprice upward faster than their funding costs. Betas are not fixed, though. During the 2022 hiking cycle they climbed to levels not seen since before the 2008 financial crisis, as customers moved cash into CDs and money market funds and banks leaned on costlier funding. Each customer who notices the gap pushes the beta up.

The franchise is both an asset and a hidden risk. Because banks count on deposits staying, many buy long-term bonds and fixed-rate loans with them. If deposits leave instead, the bank may have to sell those assets at a loss. That is what broke Silicon Valley Bank: customers pulled about $42 billion on March 9, 2023, with another $100 billion queued for the next day, together about 81% of its $175 billion in deposits, and regulators closed it on March 10. Its depositors were concentrated, connected and quick to act. AI agents threaten to make ordinary depositors behave the same way, not in a panic but in a steady drip. The three largest US banks by Slok's count hold $1.6 trillion in deposits paying nothing, and paying 3% on them would cost about $47 billion a year. That is why the banks blocked outside agents in October 2026 and why bank stocks are partly a bet on customer inertia.

Your idle cash is someone else's profit. Every dollar sitting in a near-zero checking account above what you need for bills is a loan to your bank at a rate you would never accept from a borrower. Keep a working buffer where your payments run, and put the rest where the rate tracks the market, then check it again after the Fed moves, since many accounts lag. When you evaluate a bank as a business or an investment, look at its share of non-interest-bearing deposits, how much its funding costs rose in the last hiking cycle, and how concentrated or fast-moving its depositors are: a cheap franchise is only valuable if it stays.
What rate does my checking and savings cash earn today, and what does a money market fund or Treasury bill pay?
How much do I need in my everyday account to cover bills, and where should the rest sit?
How much of this bank's funding pays no interest, and how quickly did its deposit costs rise when rates went up?
If a large share of depositors could move cash at the touch of a button, what would this bank have to sell?

title: Reading an IPO prospectus: what the S-1 really tells you
layers: An initial public offering, or IPO, is the moment a private company first sells shares to the public. To do it in the US, the company registers with the SEC, usually on Form S-1, and the core of that filing is the prospectus: the company's own account of its business, finances, risks, management and the terms of the sale. Drafts are amended as S-1/A filings, and the final prospectus with the price is filed later. The SEC reviews the document for disclosure, but, as its investor bulletin stresses, it does not judge whether the deal is a good investment. Anthropic's S-1, filed October 26, 2026, runs to hundreds of pages and is the first full public view of its finances.

The sale itself is run by underwriters, investment banks that gauge demand from big investors in a roadshow, recommend a price and are paid a percentage of the money raised. Anthropic named Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley to lead 20 other banks, with Morgan Stanley as stabilization agent, the bank allowed to buy shares in the first days to support a falling price. The SEC notes that most shares go to institutions and wealthy clients, so most individuals can only buy once trading opens. Banks also tend to price below what the market will pay: Jay Ritter's data show US IPOs from 1980 to 2025 rose 19% on average on their first day, leaving $250 billion on the table that the companies could have raised. Existing holders usually agree to a lock-up, typically 180 days, and the SEC warns that the price can drop when that many shares become free to sell at once.

Read the prospectus in layers. Start with revenue and its growth, then loss from operations, which shows whether the core business earns money, then net income, which adds items like interest and accounting revaluations. These can tell very different stories. Anthropic's revenue for the first half of 2026 was $16.3 billion against $1.2 billion a year earlier, and its operating loss shrank to $693 million. Its net loss was $80.7 billion, because $72.4 billion came from marking up convertible notes: debt that turns into shares, which became more costly on paper as the company's valuation rose. That charge reflects the valuation, not the cost of running the business, but the shares it implies are real dilution for new buyers. Next read the commitments: Anthropic reports more than $500 billion of computing contracts it largely cannot cancel, a fixed cost that stays even if revenue growth slows. Then read Risk Factors, Use of Proceeds, Dilution and Shares Eligible for Future Sale. Finally read Description of Capital Stock. Anthropic will have five share classes, its founders' class will hold 50.1% of the voting power on most matters, and a Long-Term Benefit Trust will elect a board majority, making it a controlled company under Nasdaq rules.

Treat an IPO as the start of public price discovery, not a finish line. The headline numbers in the press are the ones easiest to misread, so check operating results against net results, ask what a non-cash charge says about dilution, and size up the obligations a company cannot walk away from. Note who controls the board and how much you will be able to influence it. And remember the mechanics are tilted toward insiders and big clients: by the time you can buy, the first-day pop may already be priced in, and a lock-up expiry months later can bring a wave of new sellers. None of this tells you whether to buy; it tells you what you would be buying.
What does the company earn from operations, separate from accounting charges and interest?
Which costs and commitments can it not cancel if growth slows?
Who controls the votes and the board after the IPO, and what rights does my share class carry?
When does the lock-up expire, and how many shares could be sold then?

title: Buybacks and dividends: how companies hand cash back
layers: A profitable company that has more cash than it can invest well has three choices: keep it, pay it out as a dividend, or use it to buy back its own shares. A dividend is a cash payment to every shareholder, usually per share and on a schedule. A buyback, or share repurchase, is the company buying its stock in the market or from holders; when the bought shares are canceled, the company is split into fewer pieces and each remaining share owns a bigger slice of its profits. In the 12 months to June 2025, S&P 500 companies spent $997.8 billion on buybacks and a record $653.9 billion on dividends, per S&P Dow Jones Indices, and the 20 biggest buyers made up 51.3% of the buyback spending in the second quarter.

The arithmetic is simple. A company earning $100 million with 100 million shares makes $1.00 per share. If it buys back and cancels 10 million shares, the same $100 million spread over 90 million shares is about $1.11, an 11% rise in earnings per share with no growth in the business. S&P notes that falling share counts have lifted per-share earnings, and 17.3% of S&P 500 companies cut their share count by at least 4% in a year. Two details decide whether that slice really grows. First, cancellation: SK hynix's October 2026 plan counts only shares it buys and cancels, while a separate 10 trillion won purchase for employee pay is excluded, because shares bought to hand out again do not shrink the pie. Second, the cash spent no longer earns interest, so net income dips a little, and if the buyback is paid with debt, risk rises too. In the US, companies also pay a 1% excise tax on net buybacks, which S&P measured at about 0.4% of earnings.

The value comes from the price, not the act. If a company pays $50 for a share worth $70, the owners who stay gain; at $70 they break even; at $90 the company has transferred wealth to the sellers. This is why timing matters, and why companies often buy most when profits and cash are highest, near the top of a cycle. SK hynix shows the tension: after an 80% operating margin it pledged 100 trillion won for 2026, roughly 10% of its market value in one year by TIKR's estimate, while its finance chief said the shares were undervalued at about 3.3 times expected earnings. In a cyclical industry that low multiple can mean a bargain or can mean investors expect profits to fall. Dividends carry a different signal: once paid regularly they are hard to cut without alarming investors, so boards treat them as a promise, while buybacks can be dialed up or down each quarter. That is why SK hynix tied its future returns to a share of free cash flow, more than 50%, instead of a fixed amount.

A payout is a decision about where cash earns the most, not a gift. Judge it with a few numbers: free cash flow compared with the payout, whether debt rose to fund it, the share count over five years after employee stock awards, and the price paid compared with a sober estimate of value. A growing company may create more wealth by reinvesting than by paying out, and a mature company that hoards cash may waste it. Add the dividend yield and the net buyback yield together, often called shareholder yield, to see the full return of cash, then ask whether the profits behind it can last.
Is the share count actually falling over five years once employee stock awards are added back?
Is the payout funded by free cash flow, or by new borrowing?
Is the company buying at a price below a reasonable estimate of value, or near the peak of its profit cycle?
Would this cash earn more reinvested in the business than handed back?

title: Inside the Fed's vote: statements, dissents and the dot plot
layers: Interest rates in the US are set by a committee, not a person. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) brings together the Fed's governors in Washington and the presidents of the regional Fed banks; at each meeting a set of them vote on the target range for the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other overnight. The committee meets eight times a year. Every meeting produces three things markets read closely: the decision, a short written statement, and the chair's press conference. Some meetings also produce projections from every official, the 'dot plot,' with one dot per person for where they think rates should be. On Oct 28, 2026, the committee held rates at 3.75% to 4% by a vote of 10-2.

Each piece carries information. The decision tells you what the Fed did. The statement is negotiated word by word, so small edits matter: in October, 'raise' became 'maintain,' growth went from a 'solid' to a 'strong' pace, and 'inflation remains elevated' stayed in. Analysts line up the new statement next to the old one and read the changes as a message. The dissents tell you where the edge of the debate is: a dissent is a public vote against the chair's proposal, with a written reason. In October, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voted against holding because they wanted a quarter-point hike. In September the vote had been 12-0. The dot plot shows the middle of the committee's thinking: the latest one pointed to a second hike in 2026. The press conference adds tone. Chair Kevin Warsh said 'interest rates have had an effect' and that the goal 'isn't to throw sand in the gears of the economy.' Finally, futures markets turn all of this into odds; after this meeting traders still put about an 84% chance on a December hike.

Dissents matter because the Fed works hard to look united. A chair usually builds consensus before the vote, so even one 'no' means a real disagreement could not be bridged. When dissents all lean the same way, they often preview the next move: here both dissenters wanted tighter policy, which tells you the debate is about how high, not when to cut. Direction of dissent is the key detail. A hold with two votes for a hike is hawkish; a hold with two votes for a cut is dovish. The same decision can move markets in opposite directions depending on who voted no and why. Process changes matter too: starting in 2027 the Fed plans to keep eight meetings a year but devote one to broad strategy, and two in 2028, leaving fewer meetings where rates can change. Fewer decision points can mean larger moves when they come, and more weight on each statement.

Do not stop at the headline 'Fed holds.' Read four things: the direction of any dissents, the words that changed in the statement, where the dots sit, and what futures now price. Together they tell you whether the next move is up, down or nowhere, and that feeds straight into what you pay on a mortgage, a credit card or a business line of credit, and what you earn on cash. A personal rule: when the Fed is split toward hikes, avoid locking in variable-rate debt on the assumption that rates will soon fall.
Did anyone dissent, and did they want tighter or easier policy?
Which words in the statement changed from the last meeting, and what do the changes signal?
Do the dot plot and futures odds agree on the next move, or is the market betting against the Fed?
If rates stay where they are for another year, what does that do to my debt costs and my cash returns?

title: Free cash flow and capex: when profit is not cash
layers: Free cash flow is the cash a business has left after paying for everything it needs to keep running and growing. The formula is short: cash from operations minus capital expenditures. Cash from operations is the money that actually came in from customers, minus the cash paid out to staff, suppliers and tax collectors. Capital expenditures, or capex, are purchases of long-lived assets: buildings, machines, servers, chips, trucks. Net income, the 'profit' in headlines, is something different. It follows accounting rules that match costs to the years they help, so it can be large while the bank account shrinks. Alphabet showed the gap in its third quarter of 2026: $40.6 billion of operating income, $42.3 billion of cash from operations, $51.4 billion of capex, and free cash flow of negative $9.1 billion.

Three things pull profit and cash apart. First, depreciation. When a company buys a $1 billion data center, it does not record a $1 billion expense that year. It spreads the cost over the asset's useful life, say a slice each year for several years. The cash leaves on day one; the expense trickles into the income statement for years. That is why a company building fast shows healthy profit while its cash flow turns negative: Alphabet's depreciation was $8.4 billion in the quarter, about a sixth of what it spent on new assets. Second, working capital. Money tied up in inventory, or in bills customers have not paid yet, is real cash that has not come back. Alphabet's inventory rose from about $2.4 billion to $13.3 billion as it built chip systems for cloud customers, which absorbed cash even though the sales were contracted. Third, non-cash items. Gains and losses on investments, stock-based pay and write-downs change profit without moving cash; Alphabet booked an $8.7 billion paper loss on equity investments, which cut profit but not cash. Analysts also split capex in two: maintenance capex keeps the business where it is, and growth capex expands it. Only the second is optional, and companies rarely disclose the split, so you estimate it, often by comparing capex to depreciation. Capex far above depreciation means heavy expansion.

This matters because cash, not accounting profit, is what a company can actually use. Dividends, buybacks, paying down debt and buying other companies all require cash. When free cash flow is negative, the money has to come from somewhere: savings on the balance sheet, new borrowing, or new shares that dilute existing owners. Alphabet raised $28.7 billion of notes and $12.4 billion from share sales in the quarter and did no buybacks. Heavy investment is not bad in itself: a cloud business whose revenue grew 103% may earn excellent returns on those data centers. The question is whether the return on that spending will beat the cost of the money, and that answer arrives years later. History offers both outcomes. Railroads, telecom fiber in the late 1990s, and shale drilling all saw huge capex booms in which some builders earned great returns and others were left with debt and assets worth less than they cost. A business that needs constant heavy spending just to stay in place, called capital-intensive, also tends to be worth less per dollar of profit than one that grows with little new investment, because less of its profit can ever be handed to owners.

Read cash flow next to profit, every time. Start with the cash flow statement, not the income statement: find cash from operations and capex, and subtract. Then ask four questions. Is free cash flow positive, and is it trending up or down over several quarters? How does capex compare with depreciation: roughly equal suggests maintenance, far higher suggests a build-out whose payoff is still a bet? How is any shortfall being funded: cash on hand, debt or new shares? And does management give a clear account of the return it expects? A useful habit is the cash conversion check: divide free cash flow by net income over a few years. Mature, healthy companies usually turn most of their profit into cash; a persistent large gap deserves an explanation. Valuation metrics such as price to earnings can mislead in a spending boom, so many investors also look at price to free cash flow. Neither number alone is an answer; together they show whether the story and the cash agree.
How much of last year's profit actually turned into free cash flow, and why the difference?
Is capex well above depreciation, and what return does management say it expects from the extra spending?
If free cash flow is negative, is the gap funded from cash, debt or new shares, and for how long can that continue?
What share of my index fund sits in companies in the middle of the same spending boom?

title: Earnings guidance: why the forecast moves the stock more than the results
layers: Guidance is a company's own forecast of its coming results, usually for the next quarter and sometimes the full year. Most large US companies give it in a table at the bottom of their quarterly earnings release: a revenue range, a gross margin, and earnings per share, often in two versions, GAAP (the official accounting rules) and non-GAAP (adjusted to strip out items management considers one-off). Intel's release on October 29, 2026 is a clean example. For the fourth quarter it forecast revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, a non-GAAP gross margin of 38.0%, and non-GAAP earnings of $0.25 a share, and it stated that the margin and earnings figures assume the midpoint of the revenue range. Next to guidance sits the consensus: the average of the forecasts published by the analysts who cover the stock. For Intel's fourth quarter, analysts surveyed by LSEG expected $17.1 billion of revenue and $0.43 a share. The gap between guidance and consensus is often the real news of earnings day.

The mechanism runs through expectations. Before a report, a stock's price already reflects what investors collectively believe about future profits. Results that match those beliefs change little, because nothing new was learned. The market reacts to the surprise, the difference between what came out and what was expected, and it weighs surprises about the future more than surprises about the past, because a stock's value is the worth of all its future cash flows, not last quarter's. Intel shows both sides at once. Its third quarter beat its own guidance: revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21%, and adjusted earnings of $0.52 a share. Yet its fourth-quarter earnings forecast was roughly 42% below consensus, its revenue midpoint about 9% below, and its margin guide six points lower than the quarter just reported. Analysts then cut their models for next quarter and the quarters after it, and lower expected earnings times a lower multiple (investors pay less per dollar of profit when growth looks shakier) gives a much lower price. The stock closed 28.58% down, its worst day since 1974. Watch the pieces of a guidance table, not just the headline: a margin forecast falling faster than revenue tells you costs or pricing are under pressure; a wide range signals uncertainty; and the commentary matters. Intel's finance chief said he sees the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year, which stretches the bad news beyond one quarter. The effect also spreads: when one company warns about its market, investors reprice its suppliers, customers and competitors, which is why AMD and other chip stocks fell around 10% the same day.

This matters because it explains moves that look irrational. A company can report record growth and see its stock fall, or report a loss and see it rise, because the price was set by expectations before the news arrived. Management controls guidance, which creates incentives: many companies guide conservatively so they can 'beat' later, and analysts know it, so a small beat of a cautious guide may disappoint. Some companies stop giving guidance in uncertain times, which shifts more weight onto analyst estimates and conference-call tone. For a business owner the same logic applies to lenders and investors: they fund the plan you forecast, and missing your own forecast damages trust more than delivering a modest one you hit. For a long-term investor, a guidance shock is information about a business, not an instruction to act. The useful question is whether the forecast changed your view of the company's long-run earning power or only its next few months.

A stock moves on the gap between what happens and what was expected, and expectations about the future count most. Read the guidance table and the consensus side by side, check whether margins are falling faster than sales, and listen for how long management says a problem will last. Then separate a temporary reset in expectations from a permanent change in what the business can earn.
What did the company guide for next quarter, and how does that compare with the analyst consensus?
Is the margin forecast falling faster than the revenue forecast, and does management explain why?
Does management describe the weakness as one quarter or something that lasts into next year?
Has this company tended to guide conservatively and then beat, or to miss its own forecasts?
